entries.ac2d3805403fb94d9e7219b12c373fde5fce7993: <div sID="gen20552" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Nah.3" sID="Nah.3"/> <div eID="gen20552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20553" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20554" type="x-p"/> This chapter goes on with the burden of Nineveh, and concludes it. I. The sins of that great city are charged upon it, murder (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.1">ver. 1</reference>), whoredom and witchcraft (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.4">ver. 4</reference>), and a general extent of wickedness, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.19">ver. 19</reference>. II. Judgments are here threatened against it, blood for blood (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.2-Nah.3.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>), and shame for shameful sins, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5-Nah.3.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. III. Instances are given of the like desolations brought upon other places for the like sins, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8-Nah.3.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. IV. The overthrow of all those things which they depended upon, and put confidence in, is foretold, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.12-Nah.3.19">ver. 12-19</reference>.
entries.1ed8b8717aab370b60291c593ad190dcce7cc019: <div eID="gen20554" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20553" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Nineveh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20555" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to the bloody city! it <hi type="italic">is</hi> all full of lies <hi type="italic">and</hi> robbery; the prey departeth not; <hi type="super">2</hi> The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots. <hi type="super">3</hi> The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases; and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none end of <hi type="italic">their</hi> corpses; they stumble upon their corpses: <hi type="super">4</hi> Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the well-favoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts. <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazing-stock. <hi type="super">7</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee? <div eID="gen20555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20556" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Nineveh arraigned and indicted. It is a high charge that is here drawn up against that great city, and neither her numbers nor her grandeur shall secure her from prosecution. 1. It is a <hi type="italic">city of blood,</hi> in which a great deal of innocent blood is shed by unrighteous war, or under colour and pretence of public justice, or by suffering barbarous murders to go unpunished; for this the righteous God will make inquisition. 2. <hi type="italic">It is all full of lies;</hi> truth is banished from among them; there is no such thing as honesty; one knows not whom to believe nor whom to trust. 3. It is all full of <hi type="italic">robbery</hi> and rapine; no man cares what mischief he does, nor to whom he does it: <hi type="italic">The prey departs not,</hi> that is, they never know when they have got enough by spoil and oppression. They shed blood, and told lies, in pursuit of the prey, that they might enrich themselves. 4. There is a <hi type="italic">multitude of whoredoms</hi> in it, that is, idolatries, spiritual whoredoms, by which she defiled herself, and to which she seduced the neighbouring nations, as a well-favoured harlot, and sold and ruined <hi type="italic">nations through her whoredoms.</hi> 5. She is a <hi type="italic">mistress of witchcrafts,</hi> and by them she <hi type="italic">sells families,</hi> <reference osisRef="Nah.3.4">v. 4</reference>. That which Nineveh aimed at was a universal monarchy, to be the metropolis of the world, and to have all her neighbours under her feet; to compass this, she used not only arms, but arts, compelling some, deluding others, into subjection to her, and wheedling them as a harlot by her charms to lay their necks under her yoke, suggesting to them that it would be for their advantage. She courted them to join with her in her idolatrous rites, to tie them the faster to her interests, and made use of her wealth, power, and greatness, to draw people into alliances with her, by which she gained advantages over them, and made a hand of them. These were her whoredoms, like those of Tyre, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.15">Isa. xxiii. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">17</reference>. These were her witchcrafts, with which she unaccountably gained dominion. And for this that God has a quarrel with her who, having <hi type="italic">made of one blood all nations of men,</hi> never designed one to be a nation of tyrants and another of slaves, and who claims it as his own prerogative to be universal Monarch. <div eID="gen20556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20557" type="x-p"/> II. Nineveh condemned to ruin upon this indictment. Woe to this bloody city! <reference osisRef="Nah.3.1">v. 1</reference>. See what this woe is. <div eID="gen20557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20558" type="x-p"/> 1. Nineveh had with her cruelties been a terror and destruction to others, and therefore destruction and terror shall be brought upon her. Those that are for overthrowing all that come in their way will, sooner or later, meet with their match. (1.) Hear the alarm with which Nineveh shall be terrified, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.2">v. 2</reference>. It is a formidable army that advances against it; you may hear them at a distance, the <hi type="italic">noise of the whip,</hi> driving the chariot-horses with fury; you may hear the noise of the <hi type="italic">rattling of the wheels, the prancing horses, and the jumping chariots;</hi> the very noise is frightful, but much more so when they know that all this force is coming with all this speed against them, and they are not able to make head against it. (2.) See the slaughter with which Nineveh shall be laid waste (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.3">v. 3</reference>), the sword drawn with which execution shall be done, <hi type="italic">the bright sword lifted up and the glittering spear,</hi> the dazzling brightness of which is very terrible to those whom they are lifted up against. See what havoc these make when they are commissioned to slay: <hi type="italic">There is a great number of carcases,</hi> for the slain of the land shall be many; <hi type="italic">there is no end of their corpses;</hi> there is such <hi type="italic">a multitude of slain</hi> that it is in vain to go about to take the number of them; they lie so thick that passengers are ready to stumble <hi type="italic">upon their corpses</hi> at every step. The destruction of Sennacherib's army, which, in the morning, were <hi type="italic">all dead corpses,</hi> is perhaps looked upon here as a figure of the like destruction that should afterwards be in Nineveh; for those that will not take warning by judgments at a distance shall have them come nearer. <div eID="gen20558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20559" type="x-p"/> 2. Nineveh had with her whoredoms and witchcrafts drawn others to shameful wickedness, and therefore God will load her with shame and contempt (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.5-Nah.3.7">v. 5-7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts</hi> is <hi type="italic">against her,</hi> and then she shall be exposed to the highest degree of disgrace and ignominy, shall not only lose all her charms, but shall be made to appear very odious. When it shall be seen that while she courted her neighbours it was with design to ruin their liberty and property, when all her wicked artifices shall be brought to light, then her <hi type="italic">shame is discovered to the nations.</hi> When her proud pretensions are baffled, and her vain towering hopes of an absolute and universal dominion brought to nought, and she appears not to have been so strong and considerable as she would have been thought to be, then <hi type="italic">to see the nakedness of the land do they come,</hi> and it appears ridiculous. Then do they <hi type="italic">cast abominable filth upon her,</hi> as upon a carted strumpet, and <hi type="italic">make her vile</hi> as the offscouring of all things; that great city, which all nations had made court to and coveted an alliance with, has become a gazing-stock, a laughing stock. Those that formerly looked upon her, and fled to her, in hopes of protection from her, now <hi type="italic">look upon her and flee from her,</hi> for fear of being ruined with her. Note, Those that abuse their honour and interest will justly be disgraced and abandoned, and, because miserable, will be made contemptible, and thereby be made more miserable. When Nineveh is laid waste <hi type="italic">who will bemoan her?</hi> Her trouble will be so great, and her sense of it so deep, as not to admit relief from sympathy, or any comforting considerations; or, if it would, none shall do any such good office: <hi type="italic">When shall I seek comforters for thee?</hi> Note, Those that showed no pity in the day of their power can expect to find no pity in the day of their fall. When those about Nineveh, that had been deceived by her wiles, come to be undeceived in her ruin, every one shall insult over her, and none bemoan her. This was Nineveh's fate, when she was made a spectacle, or gazing-stock. Note, The greater men's show was in the day of their abused prosperity the greater will their shame be in the day of their deserved destruction. <hi type="italic">I will make thee an example;</hi> so Drusus reads it. Note, When proud sinners are humbled and brought down it is designed that others should take example by them not to lift up themselves in security and insolence when they prosper in the world.
entries.f3d66b8da74238a959842f2b25210208a09b4675: <div eID="gen20559" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Nineveh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20560" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, <hi type="italic">that had</hi> the waters round about it, whose rampart <hi type="italic">was</hi> the sea, <hi type="italic">and</hi> her wall <hi type="italic">was</hi> from the sea? <hi type="super">9</hi> Ethiopia and Egypt <hi type="italic">were</hi> her strength, and <hi type="italic">it was</hi> infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers. <hi type="super">10</hi> Yet <hi type="italic">was</hi> she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains. <hi type="super">11</hi> Thou also shalt be drunken: thou shalt be hid, thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy. <hi type="super">12</hi> All thy strong holds <hi type="italic">shall be like</hi> fig trees with the first-ripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater. <hi type="super">13</hi> Behold, thy people in the midst of thee <hi type="italic">are</hi> women: the gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies: the fire shall devour thy bars. <hi type="super">14</hi> Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the mortar, make strong the brick-kiln. <hi type="super">15</hi> There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts. <hi type="super">16</hi> Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and flieth away. <hi type="super">17</hi> Thy crowned <hi type="italic">are</hi> as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, <hi type="italic">but</hi> when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they <hi type="italic">are.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell <hi type="italic">in the dust:</hi> thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually? <div eID="gen20560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20561" type="x-p"/> Nineveh has been told that God is against her, and then none can be for her, to stand her in any stead; yet she sets God himself at defiance, and his power and justice, and says, <hi type="italic">I shall have peace.</hi> Threatened folks live long; therefore here the prophet largely shows how vain her confidences would prove and insufficient to ward off the judgment of God. To convince them of this, <div eID="gen20561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20562" type="x-p"/> I. He shows them that other places, which had been as strong and as secure as they, could not keep their ground against the judgments of God. Nineveh shall fall unpitied and uncomforted (for miserable comforters will those prove who speak peace to those on whom God will fasten trouble), and she shall not be able to help herself: <hi type="italic">Art thou better than populous No?</hi> <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">v. 8</reference>. He takes them off from their vain confidences by quoting precedents. The city mentioned is <hi type="italic">No,</hi> a great city in the land of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.25">Jer. xlvi. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">No-Ammon,</hi> so some read it both there and here. We read of it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.14-Ezek.30.16">Ezek. xxx. 14-16</reference>. Some think it was <hi type="italic">Diospolis,</hi> others <hi type="italic">Alexandria.</hi> As God said to Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">Go, see what I did to Shiloh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jer. vii. 12</reference>), so to Nineveh that great city, <hi type="italic">Go, see what I did to populous No.</hi> Note, It will help to keep us in a holy fear of the judgments of God to consider that we are not better than those that have fallen under those judgments before us. We deserve them as much, and are as little able to grapple with them. This also should help to reconcile us to afflictions. Are we better than such and such, who were in like manner exercised? Nay, were not they better than we, and less likely to be afflicted? Now, concerning No, observe, 1. How firm her standing seemed to be, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">v. 8</reference>. She was fortified both by nature and art, was <hi type="italic">situate among the rivers.</hi> Nile, in several branches, not only watered her fields, but guarded her wall. <hi type="italic">Her rampart was the sea,</hi> the <hi type="italic">lake of Mareotis,</hi> an Egyptian sea, like the sea of Tiberias. Her <hi type="italic">wall was from the sea;</hi> it was fenced with a wall which was thought to make the place impregnable. It was also supported by its interests and alliances abroad, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.9">v. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Ethiopia,</hi> or Arabia, <hi type="italic">was her strength,</hi> either by the wealth brought to her in a way of trade or by the auxiliary forces furnished for military service. The whole country of Egypt also contributed to the strength of this populous city; so that it was <hi type="italic">infinite, and there was no end of it</hi> (so it might be rendered); She set no bounds to her ambition and knew no end of her wealth and strength; people flocked to her endlessly, and she thought there never would be any end of it; but it is God's prerogative to be infinite. <hi type="italic">Put and Lubim were thy helpers,</hi> two neighbouring countries of Africa, Mauritania and Libya, that is, Libya Cyrenica, a country that Egypt had much dependence upon. No, thus helped, seemed to sit as a queen, and was not likely to see any sorrow. But, 2. See how fatal her fall proved to be (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet was she carried away,</hi> and her strength failed her; even she that was so strong, so secure, yet <hi type="italic">went into captivity.</hi> This refers to some destruction of that city which was then well-known, and probably fresh in memory, though not recorded in history; for the destruction of it by Nebuchadnezzar (if we should understand this prophetically) could not be made an example to Nineveh; for the reducing of Nineveh was one of the first of his victories and that of Egypt one of the last. The strength and grandeur of that great city could not be its protection from military execution. (1.) Not from that which was most barbarous; for <hi type="italic">her young children</hi> had no compassion shown them, but were <hi type="italic">dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets</hi> by the merciless conquerors. (2.) Not from that which was most inglorious and disgraceful: <hi type="italic">They cast lots for her honourable men</hi> that were made prisoners of war, who should have them for their slaves. So many had they of them that they knew not what to do with them, but they made sport with throwing dice for them; <hi type="italic">all her great men,</hi> that used to be adorned on state-days with chains of gold, <hi type="italic">were</hi> now <hi type="italic">bound in chains of iron;</hi> they were <hi type="italic">pinioned</hi> or <hi type="italic">handcuffed</hi> (so the word properly signifies), not only as slaves, but as condemned malefactors. What a mortification was this to <hi type="italic">populous No,</hi> to have her honourable men and great men, that were her pride and confidence, thus abused! Now hence he infers against Nineveh (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.11">v. 11</reference>), "Thou also shalt be intoxicated, infatuated; thou also shalt reel and stagger, as drunk with the cup of the Lord's fury, that shall be put into thy hand" (see <reference osisRef="Jer.25.17">Jer. xxv. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.27">27</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt fall and rise no more.</hi> The cup shall go round, and come to thy turn, O Nineveh! to drink off at last, and shall be to thee as the waters of jealousy." <div eID="gen20562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20563" type="x-p"/> II. He shows them that all those things which they reposed a confidence in should fail them. 1. Did the men of Nineveh trust to their own magnanimity and bravery? Their hearts should sink and fail them. <hi type="italic">They shall be hid,</hi> shall abscond for shame, being in disgrace, abscond for fear, being in distress and danger, and not able to face the enemies, because of whose strength and terror, having no strength of their own, they shall <hi type="italic">seek strength,</hi> shall come sneaking to their neighbours to beg their assistance in a time of need. Thus God can <hi type="italic">cut off the spirit</hi> of princes, and <hi type="italic">take away their heart.</hi> 2. Did they depend upon their barrier, the garrisons and strongholds they had, which were regularly fortified and bravely manned? Those shall prove but paper-walls, and <hi type="italic">like the first-ripe figs,</hi> which, if you give the tree but a little shake, will <hi type="italic">fall into the mouth of the eater</hi> that gapes for them; so easily will all their strongholds be made to surrender to the advancing enemy, upon the first summons, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.12">v. 12</reference>. Note, Strongholds, even the strongest, are no fence against the judgments of God, when they come with commission. <hi type="italic">The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and a high wall,</hi> but only <hi type="italic">in his own conceit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Prov. xviii. 10</reference>. They are supposed to make their strongholds as strong as possible, and are challenged to do their utmost to make them tenable, and serviceable to them against the invader (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Draw thee water for the siege;</hi> lay in great quantities of water, that that which is so necessary to the support of human life may not be wanting; it is put here for all manner of provision, with which Nineveh is ironically told to furnish herself, in expectation of a siege. "Take ever so much care that thou mayest not be starved out, and forced by famine to surrender, yet that shall not avail. <hi type="italic">Fortify the strongholds,</hi> by adding out-works to them, or putting men and arms into them," as with us by planting cannon upon them. "<hi type="italic">Go into clay, and tread the mortar,</hi> and <hi type="italic">make strong the brick-kiln;</hi> take all the pains thou canst in erecting new fortifications; but it shall be all in vain, for (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.15">v. 15</reference>) there shall even <hi type="italic">the fire devour thee</hi> if it be taken by storm." It is by fire and sword that in time of war the great devastations are made. 3. Did they put confidence in the multitude of their inhabitants? Were they, from their number and valour, reckoned their strongest walls and fortifications? Alas! these shall stand them in no stead; they shall but sink the sooner under the weight of their own numbers (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy people in the midst of thee are women;</hi> they have no wisdom, no courage; they shall be fickle, feeble, and faint-hearted, as women commonly are in such times of danger and distress; they shall be at their wits' end, adding to their griefs and fears by the power of their own imagination, and utterly unable to do any thing for themselves; the valiant men shall become cowards. <hi type="italic">O verè Phrygiæ, neque enim Phryges</hi>—<hi type="italic">Phrygian dames, not Phrygian men.</hi> Though they <hi type="italic">make themselves many</hi> (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.15">v. 15</reference>), as the <hi type="italic">canker-worm</hi> and <hi type="italic">as the locust,</hi> that come in vast swarms, <hi type="italic">though thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven,</hi> though thy exchange be thronged with wealthy traders, who, having so much money to stand up in defence of and so much to lay out in the means of their defence, should, one would think, give the enemy a warm reception, yet their hearts shall fail them too; though they be numerous as caterpillars, yet the fire and sword shall eat them up easily and irresistibly as the canker-worm, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.15">v. 15</reference>. They are as numerous as those wasting insects, but their enemies shall be mischievous like them. He adds (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">The canker-worm spoils,</hi> or <hi type="italic">spreads herself, and flies away.</hi> Both the merchants and the enemies were compared to canker-worms. The enemies shall spoil Nineveh, and carry away the spoil, without opposition, or any hope of recovering it. Or the rich merchants, who have come from abroad to settle in Nineveh, and have raised vast estates there, out of which it was hoped they would contribute largely for the defence of the city, when they see the country invaded and the city likely to be besieged, will send away their effects, and remove to some other place, will <hi type="italic">spread their wings</hi> and <hi type="italic">fly away</hi> where they may be safe, and Nineveh shall be never the better for them. Note, It is rare to find even those that have shared with us in our joys willing to share with us in our griefs too. The canker-worms will continue upon the field while there is any thing to be had, but they are gone when all is gone. Those that men have got by they do not care to lose by. Nineveh's merchants bid her farewell in her distress. Riches themselves are as the canker-worms, which on a sudden <hi type="italic">fly away as the eagle towards heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>. 4. Did they put a confidence in the strength of their gates and bars? What fence will those be against the force of the judgments of God? <reference osisRef="Nah.3.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">The gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thy enemies,</hi> the gates of thy rivers (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">ch. ii. 6</reference>), the flood-gates, or the passes and avenues, by which the enemy would make his entrance into the country, or the gates of the cities; these, though ever so strong and well-guarded, shall not answer their end: <hi type="italic">The fire shall devour thy bars,</hi> the bars of thy gates, and then they shall fly open. 5. Did they put a confidence in their king and princes? They should do them no service (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy crowned heads are as the locusts;</hi> those that had pomp and power, as crowned heads, were enfeebled, and had no power to make resistance, when the enemy came in like a flood. "<hi type="italic">Thy captains,</hi> that should lead thy forces into the field, are great indeed, and look great, but they are as the great <hi type="italic">grasshoppers,</hi> the <hi type="italic">maximum quod sic—the largest specimens</hi> of that <hi type="italic">species;</hi> still they are but grasshoppers, worthless things, that can do no service. <hi type="italic">They encamp in the hedges, in the cold day,</hi> the cold weather, <hi type="italic">but, when the sun arises, they flee away,</hi> and are gone, nobody knows whither. So these mercenary soldiers that lay slumbering about Nineveh, when any trouble arises, flee away, and shift for their own safety. <hi type="italic">The hireling flees, because he is a hireling.</hi>" The <hi type="italic">king of Assyria</hi> is told, and it is a shame he needs to be told it (who might observe it himself), that <hi type="italic">his shepherds slumber;</hi> they have no life or spirit to appear for the flock, and are very remiss in the discharge of the duty of their place and the trust reposed in them: Thy <hi type="italic">nobles shall dwell in the dust,</hi> and be buried in silence. 6. Did they hope that they should yet recover themselves and rally again? In this also they should be disappointed; for, when the shepherds are smitten, the <hi type="italic">sheep are scattered;</hi> the people are dispersed <hi type="italic">upon the mountains</hi> and <hi type="italic">no man gathers them,</hi> nor will they ever come together of themselves, but will wander endlessly, as scattered sheep do. The judgment they are under is as a wound, and it is incurable; there is no relief for it, "<hi type="italic">no healing of thy bruise,</hi> no possibility that the wound, which is so grievous and painful to thee, should be so much as skinned over; thy case is desperate (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.19">v. 19</reference>) and thy neighbours, instead of lending a hand to help thee, shall <hi type="italic">clap their hands over thee,</hi> and triumph in thy fall; and the reason is, because thou hast been one way or other injurious to them all: <hi type="italic">Upon whom has not thy wickedness passed continually?</hi> Thou hast been always doing mischief to those about thee; there is none of them but what thou hast abused and insulted; and therefore they shall be so far from pitying thee that they shall be glad to see thee reckoned with." Note, Those that have been abusive to their neighbours will, one time or another, find it come home to them; they are but preparing enemies to themselves against their day comes to fall: and those that dare not lay hands on them themselves will <hi type="italic">clap their hands over them,</hi> and upbraid them with their former wickedness, for which they are now well enough served and paid in their own coin. <hi type="italic">The troublers shall be troubled</hi> will be the burden of many, as it is here <hi type="italic">the burden of Nineveh.</hi>  <chapter eID="Nah.3"/> <div eID="gen20563" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen20518" osisID="Nah" type="book"/>

entries.400f0c487919b9779c9049d3fd4504be4f6b86a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12847"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Nah.3.1-Nah.3.19">Na 3:1-19</reference>. Repetition of Nineveh's Doom, with New Features; the Cause Is Her Tyranny, Rapine, and Cruelty: No-ammon's Fortifications Did Not Save Her; It Is Vain, Therefore, for Nineveh to Think Her Defenses Will Secure Her against God's Sentence.</title> <div sID="gen23921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12847"/><hi type="bold">1. the bloody city!--</hi>literally, "city of blood," namely, shed by Nineveh; just so now her own blood is to be shed.<div eID="gen23921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">robbery--</hi>violence [Maurer]. Extortion [Grotius].<div eID="gen23922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prey departeth not--</hi>Nineveh never ceases to live by rapine. Or, the Hebrew verb is transitive, "she (Nineveh) does not make the prey depart"; she ceases not to plunder. <div eID="gen23923" type="x-p"/>
entries.b45c10a818963c7a10973d17e5cbe4c71e3990e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12848"/><div sID="gen23924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12848"/>2. The reader is transported into the midst of the fight (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.47.3">Jr 47:3</reference>). The "noise of the whips" urging on the horses (in the chariots) is heard, and of "the rattling of the wheels" of war chariots, and the "horses" are seen "prancing," and the "chariots jumping," &c. <div eID="gen23924" type="x-p"/>
entries.610218e72c9fbe0aab0e5b22a16a1e3cb9eb4441: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12849"/><div sID="gen23925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12849"/><hi type="bold">3. horseman--</hi>distinct from "the horses" (in the chariots, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.2">Na 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifteth up--</hi>denoting readiness for fight [Ewald]. Gesenius translates, "lifteth up (literally, 'makes to ascend') his horse." Similarly Maurer, "makes his horse to rise up on his hind feet." Vulgate translates, "ascending," that is, making his horse to advance up to the assault. This last is perhaps better than English Version.<div eID="gen23926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bright sword and the glittering spear--</hi>literally, "the glitter of the sword and the flash of the spear!" This, as well as the translation, "the horseman advancing up," more graphically presents the battle scene to the eye.<div eID="gen23927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they stumble upon their corpses--</hi>The Medo-Babylonian enemy stumble upon the Assyrian corpses. <div eID="gen23928" type="x-p"/>
entries.a581d699addefa93eec28eae13f3c58df3ac724c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12850"/><div sID="gen23929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12850"/><hi type="bold">4. Because of the multitude of the whoredoms--</hi>This assigns the reason for Nineveh's destruction.<div eID="gen23929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the well-favoured harlot--</hi>As Assyria was not a worshipper of the true God, "whoredoms" cannot mean, as in the case of Israel, apostasy to the worship of false gods; but, her harlot-like artifices whereby she allured neighboring states so as to subject them to herself. As the unwary are allured by the "well-favored harlot's" looks, so Israel, Judah (for example, under Ahaz, who, calling to his aid Tiglath-pileser, was made tributary by him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7-2Kgs.16.10">2Ki 16:7-10</reference>), and other nations, were tempted by the plausible professions of Assyria, and by the lure of commerce (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Re 18:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.3">3</reference>), to trust her.<div eID="gen23930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">witchcrafts--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.47.9">Is 47:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12">12</reference>). Alluding to the love incantations whereby harlots tried to dement and ensnare youths; answering to the subtle machinations whereby Assyria attracted nations to her.<div eID="gen23931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">selleth--</hi>deprives of their liberty; as slaves used to be sold: and in other property also sale was a usual mode of transfer. Maurer understands it of depriving nations of their freedom, and literally selling them as slaves to distant peoples (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.2">Joe 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.6-Joel.3.8">3, 6-8</reference>). But elsewhere there is no evidence that the Assyrians did this.<div eID="gen23932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">families--</hi>peoples. <div eID="gen23933" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb58ed94fcefbb19e03b36a2a371e364ce8ced4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12851"/><div sID="gen23934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12851"/><hi type="bold">5. I will discover thy skirts upon thy face--</hi>that is, discover thy nakedness by throwing up thy skirts upon thy face (the greatest possible insult), pulling them up as as high as thy head (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.22">Jr 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.37-Ezek.16.41">Eze 16:37-41</reference>). I will treat thee not as a matron, but as a harlot whose shame is exposed; her gaudy finery being lifted up off her (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Is 47:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">3</reference>). So Nineveh shall be stripped of all her glory and defenses on which she prides herself. <div eID="gen23934" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd242ef5e7d1bf90b3e38a882b6b5fe589177487: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12852"/><div sID="gen23935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12852"/><hi type="bold">6. cast abominable filth upon thee--</hi>as infamous harlots used to be treated.<div eID="gen23935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gazing stock--</hi>exposed to public ignominy as a warning to others (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.17">Eze 28:17</reference>). <div eID="gen23936" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7f8d17de3460838bd147049c087a2860b814ba0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12853"/><div sID="gen23937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12853"/><hi type="bold">7. all ... that look upon thee--</hi>when thou hast been made "a gazing stock" (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.6">Na 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall flee from thee--</hi>as a thing horrible to look upon. Compare "standing afar off," <reference osisRef="Rev.18.10">Re 18:10</reference>.<div eID="gen23938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whence shall I seek comforters for thee?--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.19">Is 51:19</reference>, which Nahum had before his mind. <div eID="gen23939" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b3344e951abadeabd4dcf3cf303cf7d5fa58666: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12854"/><div sID="gen23940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12854"/><hi type="bold">8. populous No--</hi>rather, as Hebrew, "No-ammon," the Egyptian name for Thebes in Upper Egypt; meaning the portion or possession of Ammon, the Egyptian Jupiter (whence the Greeks called the city Diospolis), who was especially worshipped there. The Egyptian inscriptions call the god Amon-re, that is, Amon the Sun; he is represented as a human figure with a ram's head, seated on a chair (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.25">Jr 46:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.14-Ezek.30.16">Eze 30:14-16</reference>). The blow inflicted on No-ammon, described in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.10">Na 3:10</reference>, was probably by the Assyrian Sargon (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Is 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1">Is 20:1</reference>). As Thebes, with all her resources, was overcome by Assyria, so Assyrian Nineveh, notwithstanding all her might, in her turn, shall be overcome by Babylon. English Version, "populous," if correct, implies that No's large population did not save her from destruction.<div eID="gen23940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">situate among the rivers--</hi>probably the channels into which the Nile here divides (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.19.6-Isa.19.8">Is 19:6-8</reference>). Thebes lay on both sides of the river. It was famed in Homer's time for its hundred gates [Iliad, 9.381]. Its ruins still describe a circumference of twenty-seven miles. Of them the temples of Luxor and Karnak, east of the river, are most famous. The colonnade of the former, and the grand hall of the latter, are of stupendous dimensions. One wall still represents the expedition of Shishak against Jerusalem under Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.25">1Ki 14:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.2-2Chr.12.9">2Ch 12:2-9</reference>).<div eID="gen23941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose ... wall was from the sea--</hi>that is, rose up "from the sea." Maurer translates, "whose wall consisted of the sea." But this would be a mere repetition of the former clause. The Nile is called a sea, from its appearance in the annual flood (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Is 19:5</reference>). <div eID="gen23942" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a5ec4bd3610225b57e6dffcbf170cdda76797fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12855"/><div sID="gen23943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12855"/><hi type="bold">9. Ethiopia--</hi>Hebrew, Cush. Ethiopia is thought at this time to have been mistress of Upper Egypt.<div eID="gen23943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Egypt--</hi>Lower Egypt.<div eID="gen23944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her strength--</hi>her safeguard as an ally.<div eID="gen23945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it was infinite--</hi>The resources of these, her allies, were endless.<div eID="gen23946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Put--</hi>or Phut (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Ge 10:6</reference>); descended from Ham (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10">Eze 27:10</reference>). From a root meaning a bow; as they were famed as archers [Gesenius]. Probably west of Lower Egypt. Josephus [Antiquities, 1:6.2] identifies it with Mauritania (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jr 46:9</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.5">Eze 38:5</reference>).<div eID="gen23947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lubim--</hi>the Libyans, whose capital was Cyrene; extending along the Mediterranean west of Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.3">2Ch 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.8">16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.10">Ac 2:10</reference>). As, however, the Lubim are always connected with the Egyptians and Ethiopians, they are perhaps distinct from the Libyans. The Lubim were probably at first wandering tribes, who afterwards were settled under Carthage in the region of Cyrene, under the name Libyans.<div eID="gen23948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy--</hi>No's.<div eID="gen23949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">helpers--</hi>literally, "in thy help," that is, among thy auxiliaries. <div eID="gen23950" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd4db81820e96f2c32874f847fc7e8eff7466c9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12856"/><div sID="gen23951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12856"/>10. Notwithstanding all her might, she was overcome.<div eID="gen23951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast lots for her honourable men--</hi>They divided them among themselves by lot, as slaves (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.3">Joe 3:3</reference>). <div eID="gen23952" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc0f374aa758191f968d3bb7e340a076608a66dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12857"/><div sID="gen23953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12857"/><hi type="bold">11. drunken--</hi>made to drink of the cup of Jehovah's wrath (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Is 51:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">Jr 25:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hid--</hi>covered out of sight: a prediction remarkably verified in the state in which the ruins of Nineveh have been found [G. V. Smith]. But as "hid" precedes "seek strength," &c., it rather refers to Nineveh's state when attacked by her foe: "Thou who now so vauntest thyself, shalt be compelled to seek a hiding-place from the foe" [Calvin]; or, shalt be neglected and slighted by all [Maurer].<div eID="gen23954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek strength because of the enemy--</hi>Thou too, like Thebes (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.9">Na 3:9</reference>), shalt have recourse to other nations for help against thy Medo-Babylonian enemy. <div eID="gen23955" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffb5260a426de076af581cf5ae289fef41353f92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12858"/><div sID="gen23956" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12858"/><hi type="bold">12. thy strongholds--</hi>on the borders of Assyria, protecting the approaches to Nineveh: "the gates of thy land" (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.13">Na 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen23956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fig trees with the first ripe figs--</hi>expressing the rapidity and ease of the capture of Nineveh (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.28.4">Is 28:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.13">Re 6:13</reference>). <div eID="gen23957" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a7ef27945e434dcc8a76f6f007a0f4794c878ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12859"/><div sID="gen23958" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12859"/><hi type="bold">13. thy people--</hi>thy soldiers.<div eID="gen23958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">women--</hi>unable to fight for thee (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">Is 19:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">Jr 50:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.30">51:30</reference>).<div eID="gen23959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gates on thy land--</hi>the fortified passes or entrances to the region of Nineveh (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.15.7">Jr 15:7</reference>). Northeast of Nineveh there were hills affording a natural barrier against an invader; the guarded passes through these are probably "the gates of the land" meant.<div eID="gen23960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire shall devour thy bars--</hi>the "bars" of the fortresses at the passes into Assyria. So in Assyrian remains the Assyrians themselves are represented as setting fire to the gates of a city [Bonomi, Nineveh, pp. 194, 197]. <div eID="gen23961" type="x-p"/>
entries.01a53682e27dca10f759f10138ae5170f106ec2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12860"/><div sID="gen23962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12860"/>14. Ironical exhortation to Nineveh to defend herself.<div eID="gen23962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Draw ... waters--</hi>so as not to be without water for drinking, in the event of being cut off by the besiegers from the fountains.<div eID="gen23963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make strong the brick-kiln--</hi>or "repair" [Maurer]; so as to have a supply of bricks formed of kiln-burnt clay, to repair breaches in the ramparts, or to build new fortifications inside when the outer ones are taken by the foe. <div eID="gen23964" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf26deaf99eb93b53a19a4f4905802d40ae3974e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12861"/><div sID="gen23965" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12861"/><hi type="bold">15. There--</hi>in the very scene of thy great preparations for defense; and where thou now art so secure.<div eID="gen23965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire--</hi>even as at the former destruction; Sardanapalus (Pul?) perished with all his household in the conflagration of his palace, having in despair set it on fire, the traces of which are still remaining.<div eID="gen23966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cankerworm--</hi>"the licking locust" [Henderson].<div eID="gen23967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make thyself many as the locusts--</hi>"the swarming locusts" [Henderson]; that is, however "many" be thy forces, like those of "the swarming locusts," or the "licking locusts," yet the foe shall consume thee as the "licking locust" licks up all before it. <div eID="gen23968" type="x-p"/>
entries.642cdd577a3458173c7100e3acb54b6944b36af6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12862"/><div sID="gen23969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12862"/><hi type="bold">16. multiplied thy merchants--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.23">Eze 27:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.24">24</reference>). Nineveh, by large canals, had easy access to Babylon; and it was one of the great routes for the people of the west and northwest to that city; lying on the Tigris it had access to the sea. The Phoenicians carried its wares everywhere. Hence its merchandise is so much spoken of.<div eID="gen23969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the cankerworm spoileth, and fleeth away--</hi>that is, spoiled thy merchants. The "cankerworm," or licking locust, answers to the Medo-Babylonian invaders of Nineveh [G. V. Smith]. Calvin explains less probably, "Thy merchants spoiled many regions; but the same shall befall them as befalls locusts, they in a moment shall be scattered and flee away." Maurer, somewhat similarly, "The licking locust puts off (the envelope in which his wings had been folded), and teeth away" (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.9">Na 2:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Joel.1.4">Joe 1:4</reference>). The Hebrew has ten different names for the locust, so destructive was it. <div eID="gen23970" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a9d5f5ebb8203387ad2b323de4c3a399bdba80a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12863"/><div sID="gen23971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12863"/><hi type="bold">17. Thy crowned--</hi>Thy princes (<reference osisRef="Rev.9.7">Re 9:7</reference>). The king's nobles and officers wore the tiara, as well as the king; hence they are called here "thy crowned ones."<div eID="gen23971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23972" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the locusts--</hi>as many as the swarming locusts.<div eID="gen23972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy captains--</hi>Tiphsar, an Assyrian word; found also in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jr 51:27</reference>, meaning satraps [Michaelis]; or rather, "military leaders" [Maurer]. The last syllable, sar means a "prince," and is found in Belshaz-zar, Nabopolas-sar, Nebuchadnez-zar.<div eID="gen23973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the great grasshoppers--</hi>literally, "as the locust of locusts," that is, the largest locust. Maurer translates, "as many as locusts upon locusts," that is, swarms of locusts. Hebrew idiom favors English Version.<div eID="gen23974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the hedges in the cold--</hi>Cold deprives the locust of the power of flight; so they alight in cold weather and at night, but when warmed by the sun soon "flee away." So shall the Assyrian multitudes suddenly disappear, not leaving a trace behind (compare Pliny, Natural History, 11.29). <div eID="gen23975" type="x-p"/>
entries.27bbb4eb37eec19e8e313df6ad8b812343be4426: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12864"/><div sID="gen23976" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12864"/><hi type="bold">18. Thy shepherds--</hi>that is, Thy leaders.<div eID="gen23976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slumber--</hi>are carelessly secure [Maurer]. Rather, "lie in death's sleep, having been slain" [Jerome] (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.16">Ex 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.76.6">Psa 76:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall dwell in the dust--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.7.5">Psa 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.17">94:17</reference>).<div eID="gen23978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy people is scattered--</hi>the necessary consequence of their leaders being laid low (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.17">1Ki 22:17</reference>). <div eID="gen23979" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7c8eb39401346bb26d58ce623cbd2e9f8fcdfdd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12865"/><div sID="gen23980" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12865"/><hi type="bold">19. bruit--</hi>the report.<div eID="gen23980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clap the hands--</hi>with joy at thy fall. The sole descendants of the ancient Assyrians and Babylonians in the whole country are the Nestorian Christians, who speak a Chaldean language [Layard].<div eID="gen23981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?--</hi>implying God's long forbearance, and the consequent enormity of Assyria's guilt, rendering her case one that admitted no hope of restoration. <chapter eID="Nah.3"/><div eID="gen23982" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen23827" osisID="Nah" type="book"/>

entries.2d52c8d5eae9f5f966714517f2f77878657012bc: <div eID="gen35024" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35025" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35026" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35026" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35025" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35027" type="x-p"/> The prophet denounces a wo against Nineveh for her perfidy and violence. He musters up before our eyes the number of her chariots and cavalry; points to her burnished arms, and to the great and unrelenting slaughter which she spreads around her, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.1-Nah.3.3">Nah 3:1-3</reference>. Because Nineveh is a city wholly given up to the grossest superstition, and is an instructress of other nations in her abominable rites, therefore she shall come to a most ignominious and unpitied end, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.3-Nah.3.7">Nah 3:3-7</reference>. Her final ruin shall be similar to that of No, a famous city of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8-Nah.3.11">Nah 3:8-11</reference>. The prophet then beautifully describes the great ease with which the strong holds of Nineveh should be taken, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.12">Nah 3:12</reference>, and her judicial pusillanimity during the siege, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.13">Nah 3:13</reference>; declares that all her preparation, her numbers, opulence, and chieftains, would be of no avail in the day of the Lord's vengeance, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.14-Nah.3.17">Nah 3:14-17</reference>; and that her tributaries would desert her, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Nah 3:18</reference>. The whole concludes with stating the incurableness of her malady, and the dreadful destruction consequently awaiting her; and with introducing the nations which she had oppressed as exulting at her fall, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.19">Nah 3:19</reference>. <div eID="gen35027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35028" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35029" type="x-p"/> Wo to the bloody city! - Nineveh: the threatenings against which are continued in a strain of invective, astonishing for its richness, variety, and energy. One may hear and see the whip crack, the horses prancing, the wheels rumbling, the chariots bounding after the galloping steeds; the reflection from the drawn and highly polished swords; and the hurled spears, like gashes of lightning, dazzling the eyes; the slain lying in heaps, and horses and chariots stumbling over them! O what a picture, and a true representation of a battle, when one side is broken, and all the cavalry of the conqueror fall in upon them, hewing them down with their swords, and trampling them to pieces under the hoofs of their horses! O! infernal war! Yet sometimes thou art the scourge of the Lord.
entries.b25dac944305ac6ad243135836cbbf2f91a3eded: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35030" type="x-p"/> Because of the multitude of the whoredoms - Above, the Ninevites were represented under the emblem of a lion tearing all to pieces; here they are represented under the emblem of a beautiful harlot or public prostitute, enticing all men to her, inducing the nations to become idolatrous, and, by thus perverting them, rendering them also objects of the Divine wrath. <div eID="gen35030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35031" type="x-p"/> Mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms - Using every means to excite to idolatry; and being, by menace or wiles, successful in all.
entries.122f04e175d46b1ca6268950ac8f0ad83c71549b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35032" type="x-p"/> I will discover thy skirts upon thy face - It was an ancient, though not a laudable custom, to strip prostitutes naked, or throw their clothes over their heads, and expose them to public view, and public execration. This verse alludes to such a custom.
entries.ca10da58527ab123a19765d9a06eafa8a252788f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35033" type="x-p"/> I will cast abominable filth upon thee - I will set thee as a gazing-stock. This was a punishment precisely like our pillory. They put such women in the pillory as a gazing-stock; and then, children and others threw mud, dirt, and filth of all kinds at them.
entries.f09564912f8afacb82feb3d82f3724d086c2a25c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35034" type="x-p"/> Who will bemoan her? - In such cases, who pities the delinquent? She has been the occasion of ruin to multitudes, and now she is deservedly exposed and punished. And so it should be thought concerning Nineveh.
entries.64b68c93f164cbf8be388024d3f4bd9f307ba4f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35035" type="x-p"/> Art thou better than populous No - No-Ammon, or Diospolis, in the Delta, on one branch of the Nile. This is supposed to be the city mentioned by Nahum; and which had been lately destroyed, probably by the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen35035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35036" type="x-p"/> The waters round about it - Being situated in the Delta, it had the fork of two branches of the Nile to defend it by land; and its barrier or wall was the sea, the Mediterranean, into which these branches emptied themselves: so that this city, and the place it stood on, were wholly surrounded by the waters.
entries.9ab1caafa93d163c89f527f9ee8c37d456d780e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35037" type="x-p"/> Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength - The land of Cush, not far from Diospolis; for it was in Arabia, on the Red Sea. <div eID="gen35037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35038" type="x-p"/> Put and Lubim - A part of Africa and Libya, which were all within reach of forming alliances with No-Ammon or Diospolis.
entries.df7cdc637e888dc49b6c9d9e3a672cef7559daa5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35039" type="x-p"/> They cast lots for her honorable men - This refers still to the city called populous No. And the custom of casting lots among the commanders, for the prisoners which they had taken, is here referred to. <div eID="gen35039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35040" type="x-p"/> Great men were bound in chains - These were reserved to grace the triumph of the victor.
entries.01ea59f3b0f3d03e0212f3e554d1af1bbecf0a6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35041" type="x-p"/> Thy strong holds - The effects of the consternation into which the Ninevites were cast by the assault on their city are here pointed out by a very expressive metaphor; the first-ripe figs, when at full maturity, fell from the tree with the least shake; and so, at the first shake or consternation, all the fortresses of Nineveh were abandoned; and the king, in despair, burnt himself and household in his own palace.
entries.7c3c85f6732df3866cb5211f87f64ad37822dc8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35042" type="x-p"/> Thy people - are women - They lost all courage, and made no resistance. O vere Phrygiae, neque enim Phryges: "Verily, ye are Phrygian women, not Phrygian men." So said Numanus to the Trojans. Virg., Aen. ix.
entries.6a939ae8c03b9a18d2fa2dc9644e49b1edc77680: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35043" type="x-p"/> Draw thee waters for the siege - The Tigris ran near to Nineveh, and here they are exhorted to lay in plenty of fresh water, lest the siege should last long, and lest the enemy should cut off this supply. <div eID="gen35043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35044" type="x-p"/> Go into clay, and tread the mortar - This refers to the manner of forming bricks anciently in those countries; they digged up the clay, kneaded it properly by treading, mixed it with straw or coarse grass, moulded the bricks, and dried them in the sun. I have now some of the identical bricks, that were brought from this country, lying before me, and they show all these appearances. They are compact and very hard, but wholly soluble in water. There were however others without straw, that seem to have been burnt in a kiln as ours are. I have also some fragments or bats of these from Babylon.
entries.af2ed0dae9f8a87678d0111fb232f0019936f4f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen35044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35045" type="x-p"/> Make thyself many as the cankerworm - On the locusts, and their operations in their various states, see the notes on Joel 2 (note). The multitudes, successive swarms, and devastation occasioned by locusts, is one of the most expressive similes that could be used to point out the successive armies and all-destroying influences of the enemies of Nineveh. The account of these destroyers from Dr. Shaw, inserted Joel 2, will fully illustrate the verses where allusion is made to locusts.
entries.705f06497871564ca775cc6bd68acfe4e200135b: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen35045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35046" type="x-p"/> Thou hast multiplied thy merchants - Like Tyre, this city was a famous resort for merchants; but the multitudes which were there previously to the siege, like the locusts, took the alarm, and fled away.
entries.8b50d45b4816daf67ae82700bf4631bab01ddfaa: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen35046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35047" type="x-p"/> Thy crowned are as the locusts - Thou hast numerous princes and numerous commanders. <div eID="gen35047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35048" type="x-p"/> Which camp in the hedges in the cold day - The locusts are said to lie in shelter about the hedges of fertile spots when the weather is cold or during the night; but as soon as the sun shines out and is hot, they come out to their forage, or take to their wings.
entries.84b80c3f2776ca147ca2e98b4fb7fdc3849d6b8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen35048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35049" type="x-p"/> Thy shepherds slumber - That is, the rulers and tributary princes, who, as Herodotus informs us, deserted Nineveh in the day of her distress, and came not forward to her succor. <div eID="gen35049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35050" type="x-p"/> Diodorus Siculus says, lib. ii., when the enemy shut up the king in the city, many nations revolted, each going over to the besiegers, for the sake of their liberty; that the king despatched messengers to all his subjects, requiring power from them to succor him; and that he thought himself able to endure the siege, and remained in expectation of armies which were to be raised throughout his empire, relying on the oracle that the city would not be taken till the river became its enemy. See the note on <reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">Nah 2:6</reference>.
entries.811a01162f9c25b99fa2d6accec0b441c3e2e0c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen35050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35051" type="x-p"/> There is no healing of thy bruise - Thou shalt never be rebuilt. <div eID="gen35051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35052" type="x-p"/> All that hear the bruit of thee - The report or account. <div eID="gen35052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35053" type="x-p"/> Shall clap the hands - Shall exult in thy downfall. <div eID="gen35053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35054" type="x-p"/> For upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed - Thou hast been a universal oppressor, and therefore all nations rejoice at thy fall and utter desolation. <div eID="gen35054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35055" type="x-p"/> Bp. Newton makes some good remarks on the fall and total ruin of Nineveh. "What probability was there that the capital city of a great kingdom, a city which was sixty miles in compass, a city which contained so many thousand inhabitants, a city which had walls a hundred feet high, and so thick that three chariots could go abreast upon them, and which had one thousand five hundred towers, of two hundred feet in height; what probability was there that such a city should ever be totally destroyed? And yet so totally was it destroyed that the place is hardly known where it was situated. What we may suppose helped to complete its ruin and devastation, was Nebuchadnezzar's enlarging and beautifying Babylon, soon after Nineveh was taken. From that time no mention is made of Nineveh by any of the sacred writers; and the most ancient of the heathen authors, who have occasion to say any thing about it, speak of it as a city that was once great and flourishing, but now destroyed and desolate. Great as it was formerly, so little of it is remaining, that authors are not agreed even about its situation. From the general suffrage of ancient historians and geographers, it appears to have been situated upon the Tigris, though others represent it as placed upon the Euphrates. Bochart has shown that Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Ammianus Marcellinus, all three speak differently of it; sometimes as if situated on the Euphrates, sometimes as if on the Tigris; to reconcile whom he supposes that there were two Ninevehs; and Sir John Marsham, that there were three; the Syrian upon the Euphrates, the Assyrian on the Tigris, and a third built afterwards upon the Tigris by the Persians, who succeeded the Parthians in the empire of the East, in the third century, and were subdued by the Saracens in the seventh century after Christ. But whether this latter was built in the same place as the old Nineveh, is a question that cannot be decided. "There is a city at this time called Mosul, situate upon the western side of the Tigris; and on the opposite eastern shore are ruins of great extent, which are said to be those of Nineveh. "Dr. Prideaux, following Thevenot, observes that Mosul is situated on the west side of the Tigris, where was anciently only a suburb of the old Nineveh; for the city itself stood on the east side of the river, where are to be seen some of its ruins of great extent even to this day. Even the ruins of old Nineveh, as we may say, have been long ago ruined and destroyed; such an utter end hath been made of it, and such is the truth of the Divine predictions! "These extraordinary circumstances may strike the reader more strongly by supposing only a parallel instance. Let us then suppose that a person should come in the name of a prophet, preaching repentance to the people of this kingdom, or otherwise denouncing the destruction of the capital city within a few years. 'With an overflowing flood will God make an utter end of the place thereof; he will make an utter end: its place may be sought, but it shall never be found.' I presume we should look upon such a prophet as a madman, and show no farther attention to his message than to deride and despise it. And yet such an event would not be more strange and incredible than the destruction and devastation of Nineveh; for Nineveh was much the larger, stronger, and older city of the two. And the Assyrian empire had subsisted and flourished more ages than any form of government in this country; so there is no objecting the instability of Eastern monarchies in this case. Let us then since this event would not be more improbable and extraordinary than the other, suppose again, that things should succeed according to the prediction; that the floods should arise, and the enemies should come; the city should be overthrown and broken down, be taken and pillaged, and destroyed so totally that even the learned could not agree about the place where it was situated. What would be said or thought in such a case? Whoever of posterity should read and compare the prophecy and event together, must they not, by such an illustrious instance, be thoroughly convinced of the providence of God, and of the truth of his prophet, and be ready to acknowledge, 'Verily, this is the word which the Lord hath spoken; verily, there is a God who judgeth the earth?"' - See Bp. Newton, vol. i., dissert. 9.  <chapter eID="Nah.3"/> <div eID="gen35055" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen34945" osisID="Nah" type="book"/>

entries.045f2edeb32b97d6c0e5dd482eb75389262838ab: <reference osisRef="Nah.3.1">Nah 3:1</reference> <div eID="gen16632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16633" type="x-p"/> The city of blood will have the shame, which it has inflicted upon the nations, repaid to it by a terrible massacre. The prophet announces this with the woe which opens the last section of this threatening prophecy. Nah 3:1. <hi type="italic">“Woe to the city of blood! She all full of deceit and murder; the prey departs not.” ‛Ir dâmı̄m</hi>, city of drops of blood, i.e., of blood shed, or of murders. This predicate is explained in the following clauses: she all full of lying and murder. <hi type="italic">Cachash</hi> and <hi type="italic">pereq</hi> are asyndeton, and accusatives dependent upon מלאה. <hi type="italic">Cachash</hi>, lying and deceit: this is correctly explained by Abarbanel and Strauss as referring to the fact that “she deceived the nations with vain promises of help and protection.” <hi type="italic">Pereq</hi>, tearing in pieces for murder, - a figure taken from the lion, which tears its prey in pieces (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.3">Psa 7:3</reference>). לא ימישׁ, the prey does not depart, never fails. <hi type="italic">Mūsh</hi>: in the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> here, used intransitively, “to depart,” as in <reference osisRef="Exod.13.22">Exo 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.12">Psa 55:12</reference>, and not in a transitive sense, “to cause to depart,” to let go; for if <hi type="italic">‛ı̄r</hi> (the city) were the subject, we should have <hi type="italic">tâmı̄sh</hi>.
entries.38b7b12e46399cfac2f87447449c80d4358a4ee6: <reference osisRef="Nah.3.2-Nah.3.4">Nah 3:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen16633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16634" type="x-p"/> This threat is explained in Nah 3:2., by a description of the manner in which a hostile army enters Nineveh and fills the city with corpses. Nah 3:2. <hi type="italic">“The cracking of whips, and noise of the rattling of wheels, and the horse in galloping, and chariots flying high.</hi> Nah 3:3. <hi type="italic">Riders dashing along, and flame of the sword, and flashing of the lance, and multitude of slain men and mass of dead men, and no end of corpses; they stumble over their corpses.</hi> Nah 3:4. <hi type="italic">For the multitude of the whoredoms of the harlot, the graceful one, the mistress of witchcrafts, who sells nations with her whoredoms, and families with her witchcrafts.” </hi> Nahum sees in spirit the hostile army bursting upon Nineveh. He hears the noise, i.e., the cracking of the whips of the charioteers, and the rattling (<hi type="italic">ra‛ash</hi>) of the chariot-wheels, sees horses and chariots driving along (<hi type="italic">dâhar</hi>, to hunt, cf. Jdg 5:22; <hi type="italic">riqqēd</hi>, to jump, applied to the springing up of the chariots as they drive quickly along over a rugged road), dashing riders (<hi type="italic">ma‛ăleh</hi>, lit., to cause to ascend, sc. the horse, i.e., to make it prance, by driving the spur into its side to accelerate its speed), flaming swords, and flashing lances. As these words are well adapted to depict the attack, so are those which follow to describe the consequence or effect of the attack. Slain men, fallen men in abundance, and so many corpses, that one cannot help stumbling or falling over them. כּבד, the heavy multitude. The <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> יכשׁלו is to be read יכּשׁלוּ (<hi type="italic">niphal</hi>), in the sense of stumbling, as in Nah 2:6. The <hi type="italic">keri</hi> וכשׁלוּ is unsuitable, as the sentence does not express any progress, but simply exhibits the infinite number of the corpses (Hitzig). גויּתם, their (the slain men’s) corpses. This happens to the city of sins because of the multitude of its whoredoms. Nineveh is called <hi type="italic">Zōnâh</hi>, and its conduct <hi type="italic">zenūnı̄m</hi>, not because it had fallen away from the living God and pursued idolatry, for there is nothing about idolatry either here or in what follows; nor because of its commercial intercourse, in which case the commerce of Nineveh would appear here under the perfectly new figure of love-making with other nations (Ewald), for commercial intercourse as such is not love-making; but the love-making, with its parallel “witchcrafts” (<hi type="italic">keshâphı̄m</hi>), denotes “the treacherous friendship and crafty politics with which the coquette in her search for conquests ensnared the smaller states” (Hitzig, after Abarbanel, Calvin, J. H. Michaelis, and others). This policy is called whoring or love-making, “inasmuch as it was that selfishness which wraps itself up in the dress of love, and under the appearance of love seeks simply the gratification of its own lust” (Hengstenberg on the Rev.). The <hi type="italic">zōnâh</hi> is described still more minutely as טובת חן, beautiful with grace. This refers to the splendour and brilliancy of Nineveh, by which this city dazzled and ensnared the nations, like a graceful coquette. <hi type="italic">Ba‛ălath keshâphı̄m</hi>, devoted to witchcrafts, mistress of them. <hi type="italic">Keshâphı̄m</hi> (witchcrafts) connected with <hi type="italic">zenūnı̄m</hi>, as in 2Ki 9:22, are “the secret wiles, which, like magical arts, do not come to the light in themselves, but only in their effects” (Hitzig). מכר, to sell nations, i.e., to rob them of liberty and bring them into slavery, to make them tributary, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference>; Jdg 2:14; Jdg 3:8, etc. (not = כמר from כבר, to entangle: Hitzig). בּזנוּניה, with (not for) their whoredoms. <hi type="italic">Mishpâchōth</hi>, families, synonymous with עמּים, are smaller peoples or tribes (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9">Jer 25:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.32">Eze 20:32</reference>).
entries.99d0accef3f6fc72894361b6ecf0084e75909348: <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5-Nah.3.7">Nah 3:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen16634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16635" type="x-p"/> The Lord will plunge Nineveh into shameful misery in consequence. Nah 3:5. <hi type="italic">“Behold, I come to thee, is the saying of Jehovah of hosts; and uncover thy skirts over thy face, and let nations see they nakedness, and kingdoms thy shame.</hi> Nah 3:6. <hi type="italic">And cast horrible things upon thee, and shame thee, and make thee a gazing-stock.</hi> Nah 3:7. <hi type="italic">And it comes to pass, every one who sees thee will flee before thee, and say, Is Nineveh laid waste? Who will bewail her? whence do I seek comforters for thee?”</hi> Nah 3:5. <hi type="italic">a</hi> as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Nah.2.13">Nah 2:13</reference></hi>. The punishment of Nineveh will correspond to her conduct. Her coquetry shall be repaid to her by the uncovering of her nakedness before the nations (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.13.26">Jer 13:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Isa 47:3</reference>; Hos 2:5). <hi type="italic">Gillâh</hi>, to uncover. <hi type="italic">Shūlı̄m</hi>, <hi type="italic">fimbriae</hi>, the skirts, borders, or lower end of the long sweeping dress (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.28.33-Exod.28.34">Exo 28:33-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>). על פּניך, over thy countenance, so that the train when lifted up is drawn over the face. מער, a contraction of מערה, from ערה, signifies in 1Ki 7:36 an empty space, here nakedness or shame equivalent to ערוה. This thought is carried out still further in literal terms in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.6">Nah 3:6</reference>, Nah 3:7. <hi type="italic">Shiqqutsı̄m</hi>, objects of abhorrence, is used most frequently of idols; but here it is used in a more general sense for unclean or repulsive things, dirt and filth. Throwing dirt upon any one is a figurative expression for the most ignominious treatment or greatest contempt. <hi type="italic">Nibbēl</hi>, to treat contemptuously, not with words, as in Mic 7:6, but with deeds, equivalent to insult or abuse (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">Jer 14:21</reference>). To make it כּראי, the object of sight, i.e., to give up to open shame, παραδειγματίζειν (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.19">Mat 1:19</reference>). ראי, a pausal form of ראי, the seeing, here the spectacle, like θέατρον in 1Co 4:9. This is evident from <reference osisRef="Nah.3.7">Nah 3:7</reference>, where ראיך contains a play upon ראי. Every one who looks at her will flee from her as an object of disgust. שׁדּדה, a rare form of the <hi type="italic">pual</hi> for שׁדּדה (for the fact, compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.20">Jer 48:20</reference>). The last two clauses express the thought that no one will take pity upon the devastated city, because its fate is so well deserved; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.19">Isa 51:19</reference>, where the same words are used of Jerusalem. Nineveh will not be able to protect herself from destruction even by her great power. The prophet wrests this vain hope away from her by pointing in Isa 51:8. to the fall of the mighty Thebes in Egypt.
entries.a40e530a8de1ebce74e8ab7cc4e647186c766fb1: <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8-Nah.3.10">Nah 3:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen16635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16636" type="x-p"/> Nineveh will share the fate of No-Ammon. - Nah 3:8. <hi type="italic">“Art thou better than No-amon, that sat by rivers, waters round about her, whose bulwark was the sea, her wall of sea?</hi> Nah 3:9. <hi type="italic">Ethiopians and Egyptians were (her) strong men, there is no end; Phut and Libyans were for thy help.</hi> Nah 3:10. <hi type="italic">She also has gone to transportation, into captivity; her children were also dashed in pieces at the corners of all roads; upon her nobles they cast the lot, and all her great men were bound in chains.” </hi>התיטבי for התיטבי, for the sake of euphony, the imperfect <hi type="italic">kal</hi> of יטב, to be good, used to denote prosperity in <reference osisRef="Gen.12.13">Gen 12:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.40.14">Gen 40:14</reference>, is applied here to the prosperous condition of the city, which was rendered strong both by its situation and its resources. נא אמון, i.e., probably “dwelling (נא contracted from נוא, cf. נאות) of Amon,” the sacred name of the celebrated city of <hi type="italic">Thebes</hi> in Upper Egypt, called in Egyptian <hi type="italic">P</hi>-<hi type="italic">amen</hi>, i.e., house of the god <hi type="italic">Amun</hi>, who had a celebrated temple there (Herod. i. 182, ii. 42; see Brugsch, <hi type="italic">Geogr. Inschr.</hi> i. p. 177). The Greeks called it Διὸς πόλις, generally with the predicate ἡ μεγάλη (Diod. Sic. i. 45), or from the profane name of the city, which was <hi type="italic">Apet</hi> according to Brugsch (possibly a throne, seat, or bank), and with the feminine article prefixed, <hi type="italic">Tapet</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Tape</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Tepe</hi>, Θήβη, generally used in the plural Θῆβαι. This strong royal city, which was described even by Homer (<hi type="italic">Il.</hi> ix. 383) as ἑκατόμπυλος, and in which the Pharaohs of the 18th to the 20th dynasties, from Amosis to the last Rameses, resided, and created those works of architecture which were admired by Greeks and Romans, and the remains of which still fill the visitor with astonishment, was situated on both banks of the river Nile, which was 1500 feet in breadth at that point, and was built upon a broad plain formed by the falling back of the Libyan and Arabian mountain wall, over which there are now scattered nine larger or smaller fellah-villages, including upon the eastern bank Karnak and Luxor, and upon the western Gurnah and Medinet Abu, with their plantations of date-palms, sugar-canes, corn, etc. היּשׁבה בּיארים, who sits there, i.e., dwells quietly and securely, on the streams of the Nile. The plural יארים refers to the Nile with its canals, which surrounded the city, as we may see from what follows: “water round about her.” אשׁר־חיל, not which is a fortress of the sea (Hitzig), but whose bulwark is sea. חיל (for חילהּ) does not mean the fortified place (Hitzig), but the fortification, bulwark, applied primarily to the moats of a fortification, with the wall belonging to it; then, in the broader sense, the defence of a city in distinction from the actual wall (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.26.1">Isa 26:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">Lam 2:8</reference>). מיּם, consisting of sea is its wall, i.e., its wall is formed of sea.
